forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.82 represents a 2.2% premium to Street consensus of $6.67, driven primarily by continued underappreciation of Meta's AI-powered advertising efficiency gains. Over the trailing five quarters, Meta has beaten EPS expectations by an average of 16%, with the smallest beat (Q4 2025) still coming in at 8.6%. This systematic outperformance reflects analyst conservatism around the Advantage+ platform's ability to drive measurable ROAS improvements that advertisers continue to reward with higher spend. Management's Q4 2025 earnings call emphasized 'major AI acceleration' and that agents are 'starting to really work,' which I interpret as genuine product momentum rather than promotional language.

However, I am tempering my optimism relative to the historical beat pattern due to three factors: (1) the California and New Mexico legal settlements adding approximately $400M in one-time costs that will compress operating margins to approximately 39.5% versus the 41.5% Q1 2025 achieved, (2) the seasonal Q1 reset from record Q4 holiday advertising spend that typically sees sequential revenue declines of 20-25%, and (3) growing investor scrutiny of the $135B AI infrastructure spending commitment that may cause management to be more conservative in guidance. I project revenue of $45.5B (+7.5% YoY) and operating income of $18.0B versus Q1 2025's $17.55B.

The key swing factor for this quarter is whether the legal settlements represent the beginning of a recurring cost pattern or truly one-time events. If state attorneys general continue pursuing actions against Meta, this could add $100-150M per quarter to baseline operating expenses, which would necessitate revising my margin assumptions downward. Conversely, if the TikTok ban materializes in a meaningful way, Meta could see significant user time and advertiser budget share gains that would drive upside to my estimates. My conviction is medium given the uncertainty around legal costs and broader macro conditions.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.27 is 1.6% above Street consensus of $1.25, with the primary driver being tax rate normalization. Q1 2025's effective tax rate was approximately 36% (calculated from $606M tax expense on $1.68B pretax income), significantly elevated compared to Altria's guided normalized rate of approximately 23%. This anomaly was likely driven by discrete tax items related to equity investment mark-to-market adjustments and timing differences. With the tax rate expected to normalize to ~23% in Q1 2026, I project a meaningful EPS tailwind of $0.12-0.15 despite flat-to-slightly-declining revenue.

The core business fundamentals remain stable but unexciting. Cigarette volumes continue their secular decline of 3-4% annually, with Altria consistently outperforming the industry by maintaining Marlboro's premium positioning and disciplined pricing. The smoke-free transformation via on! oral nicotine and NJOY continues but remains immaterial to near-term earnings - the on!PLUS national launch on March 16, 2026 came too late to meaningfully impact Q1 results. Revenue should come in around $4.58B, down slightly from Q1 2025's $4.52B when adjusting for excise tax timing, reflecting the volume/price dynamic.

The key risk to my thesis is if tax rate normalization does not occur as expected. If discrete items or mark-to-market adjustments push the effective rate back toward 30%+, my estimate would need to come down to consensus or below. However, based on management's guidance for a 23% normalized rate and the one-time nature of Q1 2025's tax headwinds, I have medium-high confidence in my above-consensus call. The institutional buying activity (Nisa +3.6%, Shrier initiating position) suggests yield-focused investors remain constructive on the name despite secular headwinds.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.92 is 3.8% above the Street consensus of $1.85, reflecting continued conviction in MPC's ability to capture elevated crack spreads that have sustained at $17-19/bbl through March 2026. This represents a dramatic YoY improvement from the -$0.24 loss in Q1 2025, when crack spreads averaged only $10-12/bbl. The 55-75% improvement in crack spreads translates to approximately $1.5B in incremental gross profit opportunity, and MPC's demonstrated 105% margin capture (per Q4 2025 earnings call) suggests they will convert this opportunity into earnings at or above theoretical capacity. The stock hitting a new 52-week high of $252.83 on March 31, combined with significant institutional accumulation (Spire Wealth +320%, Dakota Wealth +23.5%), validates market confidence in this margin thesis.

I am incrementally raising my estimate from $1.88 to $1.92 based on three factors: (1) crack spreads remained robust through end of March despite typical seasonal softness, (2) peer refiner outages (Valero Port Arthur) continue to provide relative capacity value for MPC's Gulf Coast assets, and (3) the new CFO Maria Currie's emphasis on 'operational excellence and cost competitiveness' per the Q4 earnings call suggests continued margin discipline. The key difference versus consensus appears to be the Street's more conservative assumption on crack spread sustainability - I believe the market is underweighting geopolitical supply risks and refinery capacity tightness that should support elevated margins through Q1.

My thesis would be invalidated if: (1) crack spreads compress below $15/bbl, suggesting my geopolitical premium assumption is wrong, (2) MPC reports any significant unplanned downtime that wasn't captured in news flow, or (3) working capital build exceeds the $850M seasonal norm, suggesting demand weakness. The Q1 FCF will be weak (potentially negative) due to seasonal inventory build for spring driving season, but this is a timing issue rather than an earnings concern.

What would make me change my mind: If weekly EIA data shows crack spreads remained above historical Q1 averages for the entire quarter, or if MPC reports stronger-than-expected throughput volumes despite seasonal headwinds. Conversely, a sharper-than-expected decline in demand or inventory build would pose downside risk. My conviction is medium given the noisy nature of refining margins and potential for one-time items.

My Q3 FY26 estimate of $4.52 EPS on $90.5B revenue represents a 12% premium to Street consensus EPS of $4.04, maintaining conviction that Wall Street is structurally underestimating Microsoft's AI monetization leverage while also acknowledging Q2's non-recurring items. The critical insight is that Q2's blowout $5.16 EPS included approximately $10.7B in non-operating income (visible in the income statement as 'nonOperatingIncomeExcludingInterest'), which inflated EPS by roughly $1.15-1.25. Stripping this out, Q2's normalized EPS was closer to $4.00, which actually shows the business is tracking closer to my thesis than the headline beat suggested. For Q3, I'm projecting a return to normal non-operating income levels, which mechanically reduces EPS versus Q2 but maintains the premium to consensus.

The fundamental story remains compelling: Azure AI workloads are scaling faster than Street models, with the Morgan Stanley conference confirming management's confidence in sustaining 25%+ growth. I'm modeling Azure at 28% YoY for Q3, with Copilot contributing $1.8B in quarterly revenue (up from my prior $1.6-1.8B range) as enterprise adoption accelerates. The operating margin expansion thesis is playing out—I project 48.9% for Q3, benefiting from AI software leverage but with some normalization in SG&A spending. The Baron Capital note highlighting stock weakness despite strong fundamentals signals the market hasn't fully priced in the earnings power trajectory.

What would change my view: If Azure growth decelerates below 25% (suggesting AI demand saturation), if Copilot churn rates emerge as a concern, or if datacenter CapEx continues at Q2's elevated $30B pace rather than moderating to $25B (suggesting margin pressure ahead). The Mount Pleasant delay is noise, not signal—it's a local permitting issue, not systemic capacity problems. My confidence is medium-high given the strong Q2 foundation, but I'm moderating from my prior $4.58 estimate after properly accounting for Q2's non-recurring items.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view maintains that Wall Street's historical average of -$0.07 EPS materially overstates Q4 2025 losses because consensus fails to properly account for the demonstrably one-time nature of Q3's $64M operating expense explosion. The Q3 cash flow statement definitively shows $440.3M from common stock issuance, with associated underwriting fees (typically 5-7% or $22-31M), legal costs, and accounting fees explaining the G&A surge from $3.8M in Q2 to $41.4M in Q3. Similarly, R&D spiked to $22.6M in Q3 from $3.3M in Q2, likely reflecting accelerated program costs or milestone payments timed with the capital raise. Q4 should normalize to ~$10.5M total OpEx based on Q1-Q2 2025 run-rates.

The critical offset to operating losses is the dramatically elevated interest income from the $1.6B cash position post-raise. At current money market rates of ~4.7% annualized, NBP should generate approximately $19M in quarterly interest income, compared to just $1.8M in Q2 when the cash position was only $165M. This interest income nearly offsets my projected $10.5M in OpEx, resulting in a modest net loss of ~$7.2M or -$0.06 EPS on ~120M shares.

However, the severely delayed 10-K filing (now ~4.5 months post quarter-end without any NT filing) is increasingly concerning and represents the primary risk to my thesis. This could indicate: (1) complex accounting issues requiring restatement, (2) material weakness identification, (3) auditor disagreements, or (4) disclosure challenges related to the March 9 VIS-101 Phase 2a data call. If the filing reveals materially higher expenses or one-time charges, my estimate could be too optimistic. I would revise my view if the 10-K shows Q4 OpEx above $15M or discloses any going concern issues.

forecasts.thesis:
NBP screens as effectively pre-revenue in the provided financials (revenue is $0 in every quarter shown through Q3 2025), so Q4 2025 results should be dominated by (1) how far operating expenses mean-revert after the Q3 2025 spike and (2) the size of interest income earned on the materially larger cash/investment base established in Q3. My EPS call of -$0.08 stays slightly more conservative than the proxy consensus (-$0.07) because I assume OpEx remains elevated versus the pre-spike run-rate even as it normalizes sharply from Q3.

The key data points are the extreme quarterly volatility: operatingExpenses jumped to $64.0M in Q3 2025 from $7.1M in Q2, while interestIncome simultaneously jumped to $15.3M (from ~$1.8–$2.2M previously) as cashAndCashEquivalents rose to $1.62B. For Q4, I model operatingExpenses at $26.0M (down materially but not fully back to Q2) and interestIncome at $17.76M, yielding netIncome of -$8.24M and EPS of -$0.08 on ~103M shares.

I would change my mind if (a) evidence emerged that Q3’s expense spike was predominantly one-time and reverses closer to the Q2 level (driving EPS materially better than my -$0.08), or (b) Q4 includes another major expense event or financing-related costs that keep OpEx near Q3 levels (driving a much larger loss). Clearer quarter-specific disclosures (10-Q/10-K) would most directly constrain these swing factors.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.95 represents a 2.2% premium to the Street consensus of $0.93, driven by Nasdaq's persistent conservative guidance culture that Wall Street systematically underestimates. The company has delivered positive EPS surprises for 5 consecutive quarters with an average beat of +4.3%, yet analysts continue to model management's sandbagged guidance rather than adjusting for this predictable pattern. My variant view rests on: (1) Index Solutions strength confirmed by continued 424B2 structured product filings including the March 27 Citigroup issuance, supporting my ~$180M quarterly estimate vs Street likely modeling ~$165M; (2) Market Services benefiting from healthy February trading volumes and Nasdaq Texas traction; and (3) Financial Technology's accelerating SaaS transition providing recurring revenue visibility.

The key risk to my above-consensus call is the tax rate normalization from Q4's anomalous 10.5% to the guided ~19%. I model 19.0% for Q1 which is well understood by the market, but any deviation could move EPS by ~$0.01 per percentage point. The March 1 Investor Day reinforced strategic direction with the $3B buyback authorization and growth targets, providing confidence in capital allocation. The 21Shares TDOG ETF launch on Nasdaq and continued structured product demand demonstrate the platform's relevance in evolving market structures.

What would change my view: (1) Q1 trading volumes coming in materially below February's healthy levels; (2) Tax rate above 20% due to geographic mix; (3) Evidence of IPO pipeline deterioration beyond normal seasonal patterns. The blockchain/tokenization developments (Valinor launch, NYSE-Securitize partnership) remain competitive dynamics to monitor but have no near-term earnings impact. I maintain medium-high conviction given the predictable nature of Nasdaq's beat pattern and the supporting data from recent filings.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.46 maintains a significant 51% discount to Wall Street consensus of $0.93, representing one of the highest-conviction variant views in utility coverage. The fundamental issue is that Q1 is structurally the weakest quarter for NextEra due to: (1) Florida's mild Q1 weather reducing FPL demand, (2) wind capacity factors at seasonal lows of 28-30% constraining NEER production, and (3) the typical Q1 demand trough across both segments. Q1 2025 delivered diluted EPS of just $0.40 on revenue of $6.25B, and there is no structural catalyst to justify the 132% sequential EPS expansion from Q1 that consensus implies.

The key swing factor is interest expense normalization. Q1 2025's income statement showed an anomalous $1.77B interest expense (vs. $586M-$1.15B in subsequent quarters), which created significant drag on that quarter's earnings. I'm projecting $640M for Q1 2026, providing approximately $0.15 of YoY EPS benefit. Combined with modest rate base growth at FPL (~9% annually) and continued NEER capacity additions, I arrive at my $0.46 estimate - representing 15% YoY EPS growth from Q1 2025's $0.40 base.

What would change my view: If NextEra has executed a fundamental shift in Q1 seasonality through new contract structures, if there's an unannounced acquisition providing incremental earnings, or if the March 2026 investor meetings revealed Q1-specific guidance that I'm missing. The long-term thesis remains intact - NEE is a premier clean energy franchise with 8% adjusted EPS growth, 30GW data center pipeline, and exceptional competitive positioning. But Q1 will demonstrate the seasonal reality that Street estimates appear to ignore.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 Neogen forecast presents a MAJOR variant view from Street consensus: I'm projecting $0.10 EPS on $175M revenue versus consensus of $0.02 EPS on $210M revenue. The fundamental disconnect centers on two issues: (1) Wall Street's $210M revenue estimate appears to still assume near-full-quarter genomics contribution when the mid-quarter divestiture to Zoetis should only contribute ~6-7 weeks of genomics revenue before exit - this alone should drive revenue ~$35-40M below consensus; (2) The Street appears to be missing or significantly discounting the gain on sale from the genomics divestiture, which I estimate at ~$110M pre-tax based on the carrying value of genomics assets versus the ~$275M sale price. This gain should flow through to substantially positive EPS despite the operating loss in the transformed business.

Critically, Neogen has beaten EPS estimates by 212-267% in three of the last four quarters - suggesting either systematic guidance sandbagging or that Street models consistently miss key items. The recent 8-K filed March 30 (same day quarter ended) signals transaction completion and cleanup activities like the CLO departure, reducing execution risk to zero. However, I acknowledge significant uncertainty around the exact accounting treatment of the gain - GAAP rules around asset sales can result in partial deferrals or different tax treatments that could meaningfully shift EPS. My $0.10 estimate assumes the gain is largely recognized in Q3 with a blended 20% effective tax rate.

What would change my view: (1) If the gain is deferred to Q4 or partially allocated to escrow, EPS could be materially lower; (2) If transaction costs exceeded my $3-5M estimate significantly; (3) If underlying Food Safety/Animal Safety performance deteriorated beyond my assumptions. The 929% institutional accumulation by SG Americas and continued ArrowMark/Hudson Bay positions suggest sophisticated investors see the value the Street is missing. I'm adjusting my EPS estimate upward from my previous $0.05 to $0.10 based on reanalysis of the gain magnitude and Neogen's consistent pattern of significantly beating estimates.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.48 represents a 6.4% premium to the Street consensus of $6.09, reflecting conviction that analysts remain systematically conservative following the anomalous Q1 2025 EAC charge that caused a -47% earnings surprise. The subsequent four quarters delivered consistent beats averaging +10.8% surprise (Q2 2025: +19.9%, Q3 2025: +18.7%, Q4 2025: +3.9%), demonstrating the Street's persistent underestimation of NOC's normalized earnings power. With the $95.7B record backlog providing 2.4x annual revenue coverage, and B-21 production acceleration as the primary growth catalyst, I see clear visibility to continued outperformance.

The key driver of my variant view is margin normalization. Q1 2025's operating margin was depressed to 6.0% due to the one-time EAC adjustment. I project Q1 2026 operating margin at ~9.2%, consistent with the trailing three quarters (Q2: 13.8%, Q3: 11.9%, Q4: 8.9% - Q4 lower due to typical year-end true-ups). This 320bps margin improvement on ~$9.9B revenue translates to ~$317M incremental operating income versus the Street's likely conservative extrapolation from the weak Q1 2025 base. The Talon IQ autonomy flight validation with Shield AI Hivemind software adds further confidence in Aeronautics execution.

The primary risk to my thesis is another material EAC adjustment on the Sentinel ICBM program, which news characterized as 'in limbo.' However, I assign this low probability given: (1) management's explicit Q4 2025 commentary that program risks are being actively managed, (2) no new negative disclosures in recent 8-K filings, and (3) the fact that major EAC charges typically occur at year-end rather than Q1. If Sentinel experiences a material charge similar to Q1 2025, my estimate would need to be revised down ~$0.50. I would also reconsider if defense budget uncertainty materializes into actual program delays or if management signals margin pressure on the Q1 call.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.58 is $0.20 below Wall Street consensus of $2.78, representing a 7.2% downside variance. The key differentiated insight remains that the steel pricing recovery embedded in consensus expectations is overly optimistic. Commercial Metals' Q2 2026 results demonstrated weather-related disruptions and weaker-than-expected pricing metrics that directly translate to Nucor's operating environment. Additionally, Quanex Building Products' Q1 2026 results showing adjusted losses and EBITDA decline confirm ongoing weakness in the building products end-market that represents a meaningful portion of Nucor's downstream demand.

The Street appears to be extrapolating the Q3 2025 recovery (EPS of $2.63) too aggressively into Q1 2026, ignoring the Q4 2025 trough ($1.64 EPS) that revealed structural cost pressures. Specifically, SG&A spiked to $334M in Q4 from a $300M run-rate, and management has not adequately explained whether this represents one-time items or a new cost base. I'm modeling $315M SG&A for Q1, which is above historical norms but acknowledges some normalization from Q4. The UBS upgrade to Buy with a $190 price target is focused on medium-term infrastructure tailwinds and valuation support, not near-term earnings execution.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of HRC spot pricing recovery above $900/ton, which would indicate stronger-than-modeled ASP improvement, (2) Clear management commentary that Q4 SG&A spike was non-recurring with quantified items, or (3) Signs that residential construction is stabilizing faster than Quanex results suggest. My conviction is medium-high given the consistency of negative pricing signals across multiple peer datapoints, though the magnitude of the variance versus consensus introduces execution risk to my below-consensus call.

Conversely, if demand weakens more than seasonal patterns suggest, the downside risk is toward the low end of guidance at $2.70.

forecasts.thesis:
I am revising my Q1 2026 EPS estimate upward from $0.68 to $0.72, while maintaining a below-consensus view versus the Street's $0.77. The 6.5% variant stems from my assessment that Q1 represents a structural seasonal trough for Pfizer's COVID-related products that consensus continues to underweight. While the company has delivered an impressive 5-quarter beat streak averaging +34% surprises, I believe this pattern was significantly driven by favorable tax benefits and one-time items rather than sustainable operational outperformance. The normalization of the effective tax rate from negative territory to a more normalized ~1% will create a meaningful headwind that Street estimates don't adequately capture.

The upward revision from my prior $0.68 estimate reflects three factors: (1) stronger institutional accumulation signals - Capital Advisors increasing stake 6.9%, QSM Asset Management +10%, Alabama Retirement +12.3% - suggest improving fundamental views from sophisticated investors, (2) positive Phase 3 results for the Lyme vaccine and prostate cancer therapy provide pipeline optionality not fully reflected in near-term estimates, and (3) oncology momentum appears stronger than I previously modeled based on the prostate cancer trial readouts. However, I remain cautious due to the BridgeBio Attruby FDA approval creating competitive pressure on Pfizer's ATTR-CM franchise and the persistent Q1 seasonality in vaccination demand.

What would change my view: If COVID product revenue materially exceeds $3.5B (implying sustained off-season demand), or if management signals continued extraordinary tax benefits, I would revise upward toward consensus. Conversely, if the Attruby competition proves more disruptive or working capital deteriorates significantly, downside to $0.65 is possible. My medium-high conviction reflects reasonable visibility into segment dynamics offset by tax rate uncertainty and competitive dynamics.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast of $0.27 EPS on $1.49B revenue represents a 23% premium to Wall Street's $0.22 consensus, grounded in three structural factors the Street continues to systematically underweight. First, Palantir's AIP commercial acceleration represents a fundamentally different growth paradigm than traditional enterprise software - the bootcamp-to-production conversion model generates faster time-to-value and higher conversion rates than Street models assume. Q4's US Commercial segment grew 64% QoQ to ~$495M, and while I'm conservatively projecting 15-20% QoQ growth for Q1 (to $580M), even this deceleration implies 60%+ YoY growth that consensus fails to capture. The $11.2B backlog combined with the $10B Army contract provides exceptional revenue visibility that de-risks my estimates.

Second, Wall Street consistently underestimates Palantir's operating leverage potential. With gross margins already at 84%+ and SBC normalizing (I project 12.3% of revenue vs 13.9% in Q4), the incremental margin on AIP revenue is extraordinarily high. My 41.2% operating margin projection may actually prove conservative given software mix improvement and fixed cost leverage. The Street's $0.22 consensus implies roughly 38% operating margins, which fails to capture the structural margin expansion embedded in Palantir's platform economics.

Third, the 8-quarter consecutive beat streak with an average surprise of +14.5% suggests the Street has a systematic bias toward underestimating Palantir. This isn't random - it reflects difficulty modeling AIP's enterprise adoption curve and government contract execution. What would change my view: (1) evidence of AIP deal cycle elongation from macro headwinds, (2) government budget impairment beyond CR noise, or (3) competitive pressure from hyperscaler AI offerings. None of these risks are evident in current data, which supports maintaining my variant view with high conviction.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains 40% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.05, maintaining this variant view for the thirty-second consecutive analysis period. The fundamental constraint the Street continues to underestimate is Richardson Electronics' structural inability to generate operating leverage on its fixed SG&A base of approximately $15.7M per quarter. This pattern has been remarkably consistent—Q2 2026 posted a net loss of -$0.01 on $52.3M revenue with $15.9M SG&A, and even in the profitable quarters like Q1 2026 (EPS $0.13), this required the company to execute near-flawlessly on both revenue ($54.6M) and cost control ($16.0M SG&A).

The Street's $0.05 consensus implies roughly $600-650K in net income, which would require either a meaningful revenue beat above $54M or SG&A discipline below $15.5M—neither of which appears likely based on available data. RF Industries' Q1 2026 results (March 16) showed stabilization but not acceleration in the RF component channel, suggesting PMT recovery will be gradual rather than sharp. The LaserSlat SAVER product launched March 10 but is only 22 days old and unlikely to contribute meaningfully to Q3 results. My $53.2M revenue estimate represents modest 1.7% sequential growth as destocking subsides, but this level of revenue historically supports only ~$0.03-0.04 EPS when SG&A runs at the expected $15.7M level.

What would change my view: Evidence of SG&A reduction below $15.5M, revenue acceleration above $55M driven by new product traction, or a meaningful PMT order inflection that suggests the destocking cycle has definitively ended. None of these catalysts are visible in current data or management commentary from the January 8 10-Q filing.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 RGP forecast of $0.04 EPS on $106M revenue remains unchanged from prior analysis, as we are now 7 days from the April 8 earnings release with no material new developments. The core investment thesis centers on the mechanical flow-through of restructuring benefits: Q2's elevated SG&A of $54.4M included substantial severance charges from the January workforce reduction, which should normalize to approximately $44M in Q3, representing ~$10M in sequential cost savings. This cost reduction, combined with a ~$4.5M tax benefit from accumulated losses, should bring EPS to near-breakeven despite continued revenue headwinds.

The Street consensus of $0.04 EPS appears reasonable given the restructuring dynamics, and I see no compelling evidence to deviate materially in either direction. The key uncertainty remains the pace of revenue decline - I'm modeling -10% QoQ to $106M, but the enterprise consulting market remains soft and could surprise to the downside. The recent CIO hire (Prashant Lamba) and Digital Experience leadership promotion (Danielle Custalow) signal management's commitment to the strategic pivot toward AI/digital/ERP transformation services, but these won't be material contributors until FY2027.

What would change my view: (1) Any indication that restructuring savings are being reinvested rather than flowing to the bottom line would make me more bearish; (2) Evidence of enterprise consulting demand stabilization (unlikely given macro backdrop) would make me modestly more bullish on revenue; (3) Tax benefit uncertainty is the largest swing factor - if effective tax rate is less favorable than my -76% assumption, EPS could miss significantly.

My Q3 FY26 forecast for RPM International remains SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENTIATED from the stated Wall Street consensus of $0.37 EPS on $1.93B revenue, projecting $0.36 EPS on $1.51B revenue. The ~$420M (22%) revenue gap represents what I believe is a data anomaly in the consensus figure rather than genuine analyst disagreement. RPM's fiscal Q3 (Dec-Feb) is consistently their weakest quarter due to construction and consumer seasonality - Q3 FY25 generated just $1.48B revenue vs. $2.08-2.11B in the surrounding quarters. My $1.51B estimate implies modest 2% YoY growth, which is appropriate given: (1) Consumer Group headwinds from weak housing/DIY demand, (2) moderate Construction Products growth from stable commercial backlogs, and (3) continued MAP 2025 margin discipline.

Looking at Q3 FY25 ($1.48B revenue, $0.35 EPS) and applying reasonable growth assumptions (+2% revenue, modest margin improvement), we arrive at approximately $1.51B and $0.36 EPS. The Street's $1.93B figure would require 30% YoY revenue growth - entirely inconsistent with management commentary, segment trends, and the January 7 Q2 results which showed $1.91B with -19.5% EPS surprise. My EPS estimate of $0.36 is slightly below the $0.37 consensus, reflecting conservatism on Consumer Group performance and limited operating leverage in the seasonal trough.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that RPM completed a material acquisition that closed in Q3 and would add significant revenue - the March 5 8-K needs monitoring though prior reviews found no M&A disclosure; (2) Primary data showing the $1.93B consensus reflects actual analyst estimates rather than a data aggregation error; (3) Management commentary suggesting unusual strength in any segment. forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.46 remains 13.2% below Street consensus of $0.53, reflecting my conviction that Wall Street continues to systematically underestimate the velocity of net interest income compression in Saratoga's floating-rate portfolio. The key variant perception centers on the lagged impact of Fed rate cuts - while Q3 showed NII at $16.8M (already down 17% from Q2's $20.3M), Q4 will bear the full brunt of rate resets across the 85%+ floating-rate portfolio. My bottom-up analysis projects Q4 NII at $12.7M, representing a 24% sequential decline that the Street appears slow to model.

The dividend sustainability crisis is the critical overhang that consensus appears to be ignoring. At $0.75/quarter on 16.55M projected shares, the dividend requires ~$12.4M quarterly while I project net income of only $7.65M - implying a 160%+ payout ratio. Cash has declined from $148M (Q4 2025) to $52M (Q3 2026), and I project it falling to ~$24M by Q4 end. The $50M senior notes issuance announced in January provides temporary liquidity but adds ~$3.6M annual interest expense and doesn't address the core income/payout mismatch. A dividend cut within the next 1-2 quarters appears increasingly likely.

What would make me change my view: (1) Evidence that portfolio company health is generating fee income above $4M quarterly to offset NII compression; (2) Fed signaling rate pause that slows floating-rate reset velocity; (3) Management proactively reducing dividend to sustainable levels, preserving cash and NAV. The March 18 dividend declaration at $0.75 maintained suggests management is prioritizing near-term yield support over long-term balance sheet health, which reinforces my bearish stance.

My thesis centers on continued operating margin compression that consensus appears to underweight. The historical data shows clear deterioration from 5.0% operating margin in Q2 2026 (¥12.68B operating income on ¥254.43B revenue) down to 4.2% in Q3 2026 (¥10.42B on ¥249.51B). I project this 4.2% margin persists into Q4 driven by structural labor cost inflation in Japan's tight retail labor market and elevated inventory levels (¥101.3B in Q3, up 8% from Q2) creating markdown pressure.

The severe data quality issues in the available financials significantly limit my analytical confidence, which I rate as low. The Q1 2026 data appears to be denominated in USD rather than JPY (revenue of $1.70B vs ~¥250B for other quarters), making trend analysis unreliable. Furthermore, the cash flow statement is completely empty for recent quarters, preventing proper free cash flow and working capital analysis. All retrieved news articles relate to completely unrelated companies (SGC/Superior Group and SIGI/Selective Insurance), providing zero company-specific intelligence.

What would make me change my view: (1) Evidence that Q3's margin compression was one-time rather than structural, (2) Any company-specific news indicating better-than-expected same-store sales or successful price increases, (3) Resolution of the data quality issues revealing different underlying trends. Given the lack of information, I'm maintaining my conservative below-consensus stance rather than herding toward Street estimates without supporting evidence.

My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.12 EPS on $19.5M revenue represents a SIGNIFICANT DIVERGENCE from the stated $0.27 consensus, which I maintain is a stale data artifact that has not been properly updated following the Q3 FY2025 $77.2M goodwill impairment. Post-impairment, Simulations Plus has fundamentally reset its earnings power - the last two quarters delivered $0.03 and -$0.03 EPS respectively, nowhere near the $0.27 level that would require approximately $5.4M net income. My estimate implies net income of ~$2.4M, which represents a meaningful improvement from Q1's $0.68M but remains consistent with the company's normalized post-impairment profitability profile.

The key revenue drivers supporting my $19.5M estimate are: (1) stable software revenue of ~$12M supported by ongoing FDA and NIEHS contract relationships, and (2) services revenue recovery to ~$7.5M from Q1's depressed ~$6.4M level, aided by the $5.7M deferred revenue balance available for recognition. Operating margins should improve to approximately 11% as R&D expenses normalize from Q1's elevated $3.0M to ~$2.5M. The favorable tax position (NOLs from the impairment quarter) should keep the effective rate near 2%, supporting the EPS uplift.

What would change my view: If reliable evidence emerged that the $0.27 consensus reflects genuine, updated analyst expectations rather than stale pre-impairment estimates, I would need to fundamentally reassess. Additionally, if services revenue fails to recover and remains near Q1's $6.4M level, my revenue and EPS estimates would need to come down by approximately 5-10%. The institutional buying activity (First Light +115%, Royce +31.6%) suggests sophisticated investors see value at current levels, which provides some validation of the thesis that earnings are temporarily depressed rather than permanently impaired.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.38 represents a 5.6% premium to Wall Street consensus of $0.36, with the primary alpha source being the mechanical EPS accretion from management's aggressive share repurchase program that the Street appears to be systematically underweighting. The Q1 10-Q confirmed treasury stock surging from $129.3M to $230M, representing ~$99.6M in buybacks that retired approximately 6.3M shares. With the stock now trading at 52-week lows around $14, buyback math is extraordinarily favorable - I estimate an additional ~$60M repurchased in Q2 at current prices, retiring another ~4.3M shares. This would reduce diluted share count to approximately 77M versus the Street's stale assumption closer to 95-99M based on trailing averages.

The operational picture shows predictable divergence: Quest brand maintains its +9% growth trajectory supported by the protein megatrend (validated by Jefferies' recent upgrade), while Atkins continues its ~10% decline as confirmed by March 30 news citing 10-13% retail sales drops. Revenue of $345M reflects typical Q2 seasonality (historically 5% below Q1) and represents a roughly flat year-over-year comparison as Quest gains offset Atkins declines.

If actual diluted shares come in at 77M versus consensus assumption of ~96M, that alone bridges the gap between consensus $0.36 and my $0.38 estimate. The risk to this thesis is if buyback activity slowed materially in Q2 or if Atkins decline accelerated beyond the already-baked-in -10%. The March 25th TurboQuant announcement represents a legitimate long-term headwind to enterprise storage demand, but the 12-18 month adoption cycle means Q3 remains largely insulated. Analyst community reactions (Morgan Stanley defending overweight, BofA maintaining $900 target) suggest institutional conviction in the fundamental thesis despite near-term volatility.

What would change my view: evidence of accelerated TurboQuant adoption affecting Q3 LTA negotiations, gross margin guidance below 50%, or management commentary on share count methodology that contradicts my assumptions. forecasts.thesis:
My variant view remains that Q1’26 is primarily an “expense normalization” quarter rather than a heroic top-line call. The Street is anchored to a ~$1.07 EPS baseline, but I see slightly better-than-consensus EPS potential driven by otherExpenses stepping down sharply from Q4’25’s extraordinary $4.92B level toward a more typical ~$0.90B, while holding R&D/SG&A close to recent run-rate.

On revenue, the provided news is mostly regulatory/narrative without quantified Q1 sales read-through; therefore I stay seasonality-led and model $11.55B revenue (up from $10.61B in Q1’25). Incremental label/regulatory items (e.g., Rezurock EU nod) are treated as immaterial for Q1’s reported numbers.

I would change my view if the quarter includes another large discrete charge (restructuring, litigation, impairment, or expensed IPR&D) that pushes otherExpenses materially above ~$1.5B, or if vaccines timing is meaningfully weaker than seasonal expectations—either would compress operating income and pull EPS below consensus.

Vaccines shipment timing can shift revenue by ~$0.3B–$0.5B quarter-to-quarter without changing underlying demand.
FX translation and tax rate volatility could swing EPS by ~$0.05–$0.10.
margin_factors: Gross margin stable-to-slightly better vs Q1’25 on mix; COGS ~26% of revenue.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast of $2.88 EPS on $4.92B revenue represents a 1.4% beat versus Street consensus of $2.84 EPS. The key variant view is that STLD's March 18, 2026 guidance announcement explicitly projected 'higher Q1 earnings on demand and pricing gains,' yet consensus appears to have only modestly revised upward. I believe the Street is underweighting three factors: (1) the seasonal shipment recovery will be stronger than typical given robust fabrication backlog and infrastructure demand pull-through, (2) the Sinton facility's continued ramp is driving meaningful operating leverage that will expand margins beyond the 11.8% gross margin seen in Q4, and (3) management's 6% dividend increase signals confidence in near-term cash generation that hasn't been fully priced into estimates.

The quantitative support for my thesis comes from several data points. First, Q4's gross profit of $522M on $4.41B revenue (11.8% margin) was depressed by lower shipments and year-end inventory build; Q3 showed 15.7% gross margin on higher volumes, and I model Q1 returning toward 14.8% on the seasonal recovery. Second, CMC's Q2 miss of $0.12 EPS demonstrates that operational efficiency matters in this environment - STLD's diversified model and lower cost structure should enable outperformance versus weaker peers. Third, the continued institutional accumulation (SG Americas adding 61,805 shares in Q4) and KeyBanc's Overweight initiation with $190 target suggest sophisticated investors see upside the consensus is missing.

What would change my view: If March/early April HRC pricing data shows deterioration below $760/ton, or if management's Q1 call reveals that the guidance announcement was overly optimistic due to one-time factors, I would revise down to consensus. The tariff benefit remains a wildcard - my base case assumes minimal Q1 impact with benefits accruing in Q2+, but earlier implementation could provide upside. Share count is also a swing factor; my model assumes ~129M diluted shares but if buyback pace accelerates, EPS could exceed $2.90.

risks: Tariff implementation timing uncertainty could shift benefits to Q2+
Inventory build in Q4 ($3.74B vs. $3.20B QoQ) may pressure working capital
Interest expense elevated after Q4 debt issuance ($27M run-rate)
margin_factors: Operating leverage from higher shipment volumes improving fixed cost absorption
Sinton facility ramp continues to reduce per-ton costs
Metal spread compression risk manageable given scrap price stability
SG&A expected to normalize after Q4 spike to $212M
revenue_drivers: Steel operations shipments: +8-10% QoQ seasonal recovery to ~2.95M tons vs. Q4's ~2.73M tons
HRC pricing stabilization at $780-790/ton (slight improvement from late Q4 $775 levels)
Metals recycling: stable ferrous scrap flows with modest pricing support

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 diluted EPS forecast is $2.76 versus the cached Street consensus of $2.84 (a modest miss). The differentiated view is that consensus is leaning too hard into a clean, immediate margin step-up from improving steel prices, while STLD’s realized pricing typically lags spot and scrap/metal spreads can remain choppy into quarter-end—limiting the probability of a clear beat even with a strong sequential rebound.

I model revenue of $4.90B (up from Q4 2025’s $4.41B) with gross margin recovering to ~15% as steel spreads normalize and volumes improve, while SG&A stays near run-rate. The setup supports a large sequential EPS rebound, but not enough to comfortably clear $2.84 without either (1) better-than-normal price realization timing or (2) unusually favorable recycling spreads.

I would change my view if evidence emerges of faster realized pricing capture (contracts/spot pass-through) or clearly improved metal spreads late in the quarter; conversely, a sharper working-capital build (inventory at higher costs) would increase downside risk to margins and near-term earnings quality.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of $2.01 remains 16% above the Street consensus of $1.73, driven by three mechanical factors that operate largely independent of top-line uncertainty. First, SG&A normalization from Q3's elevated $491M to ~$355M represents the key swing factor - Q3 included one-time restructuring charges and Wine & Spirits transition costs that should not repeat. The CEO transition (Nicholas Fink named March 8) may add ~$10M in executive compensation but does not justify the $136M SG&A delta. Second, the accelerated share repurchase program at depressed valuations (stock trading ~$150 vs. historical ~$250) mechanically drives EPS accretion even without earnings growth - I model 170.8M diluted shares vs. Q3's 174.5M. Third, declining interest expense (~$82M vs. $86.6M in Q3) from debt paydown provides incremental support.

The Street appears anchored on negative sentiment from the Wine & Spirits divestiture and CEO transition, creating a valuation discount driven by narrative rather than fundamentals. The March 11 news about 'softer demand' and management transition has likely caused analysts to model elevated SG&A persisting, when the reality is that Q3's levels included significant non-recurring items. Beer segment fundamentals remain solid - the March 6 news confirms Pacifico and Victoria growth focus, which diversifies away from Modelo maturation concerns.

What would change my view: If Q4 SG&A comes in above $400M, that would signal either (a) CEO transition costs are materially higher than expected, or (b) there are operational issues in the beer business requiring elevated marketing spend. Additionally, if beer volumes decline more than 2% sequentially, that would signal consumer weakness beyond seasonal patterns and undermine the 53%+ gross margin assumption. The April 8 earnings release will definitively test this thesis.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 remains 6.9% above Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven by the market's systematic underappreciation of Seven & i's aggressive share count reduction program. The mathematical evidence is compelling: shares outstanding have declined from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 - a 6.2% reduction in just three quarters. I project continued buyback activity reducing shares to 2.38B by Q4 end, representing mechanical EPS accretion that consensus models appear to be missing. My ¥89.5B Q4 buyback assumption is deliberately conservative compared to Q3's ¥162.5B pace, building in cushion for potential slowdown.

The key uncertainty remains gross margin trajectory. Q3's 29.1% gross margin was anomalously high compared to the 19-20% range in Q1-Q2, likely reflecting favorable product mix and timing effects. I'm conservatively modeling 26.5% for Q4, which still represents margin compression but acknowledges that some Q3 dynamics may persist. If gross margin reverts closer to 20%, my EPS estimate would need to come down materially (to the ¥34-35 range), but the share count tailwind would still likely keep results above consensus.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that buyback authorization has been paused or significantly slowed due to Couche-Tard negotiations; (2) Q4 gross margin data suggesting return to Q1-Q2 levels rather than mid-point normalization; (3) Material deterioration in US convenience store same-store sales suggesting consumer spending weakness. The news flow since March 31 has been minimal for Seven & i specifically, with VS&Co results providing only tangential consumer spending signal. I'm maintaining my medium-high conviction given the mechanical nature of the share count alpha driver.

forecasts.thesis:
My ¥39.0 EPS estimate for Seven & i Holdings Q4 FY2026 is maintained, reflecting a balanced view of stable core convenience store operations offset by margin normalization. The key differentiation from the clearly erroneous Wall Street consensus of $0.19 (which appears to be a currency/data error) lies in my fundamental yen-denominated analysis. Q4 should benefit from seasonal strength in Japan's February year-end period and continued resilience in North American consumer spending, confirmed by VS&Co's strong FY25 results showing 5% sales growth through January 2026.

The primary earnings drivers remain: (1) Japan convenience store SSS growth of approximately 2.5%, supported by traffic recovery and modest inflation pass-through; (2) North America 7-Eleven maintaining 2-3% SSS growth amid healthy consumer backdrop; and (3) significant EPS accretion from the aggressive share repurchase program that has reduced shares outstanding from 2.60B to an expected 2.35B over the fiscal year. However, I expect gross margins to normalize to approximately 25% from Q3's elevated 29% level, which provides a meaningful headwind to absolute net income despite revenue growth.

The key risk to my thesis is the ongoing Couche-Tard acquisition uncertainty, which could create management distraction and affect strategic decisions. Additionally, any material weakening in US consumer spending would disproportionately impact earnings given North America's significant contribution. I would revise my estimate upward if gross margins prove stickier than expected or if the buyback pace accelerates further. Conversely, I would reduce estimates if US same-store sales weaken materially or if restructuring charges emerge from the superstore segment.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains 7.3% below Wall Street consensus of $0.55, anchored in the mechanical reality of tax rate normalization that I believe analysts are systematically underweighting. Q4 2025's reported EPS of $0.52 benefited from an anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income), which management explicitly attributed to discrete, non-recurring tax benefits. With management's full-year 2026 ETR guidance of 21%, Q1 tax expense should approximate $977M on ~$4.65B pretax income - a nearly $870M headwind versus Q4. This alone accounts for ~$0.12 of EPS pressure that the Street appears to be smoothing over.

The underlying business remains stable but uninspiring. Mobility service revenue should grow low-single-digits YoY driven by continued postpaid net adds and modest ARPU expansion, while equipment revenue faces the typical 30-35% seasonal decline from Q4's holiday peak. The fiber buildout continues to drive Consumer Wireline growth, with ~250K quarterly net adds expected, though OneConnect's March 31 launch is too late to impact Q1 financials meaningfully. Business Wireline's secular decline continues at roughly 4% annually. Total revenue of ~$30.55B represents essentially flat YoY performance.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) management signals additional discrete tax benefits materializing in Q1, (2) equipment revenue proves more resilient than seasonal patterns suggest, or (3) promotional activity proves less aggressive than feared. However, the tax normalization math is mechanical and well-documented in AT&T's 10-K filing, making this a high-confidence call on a specific driver that consensus appears to be mispricing.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, reflecting a fundamentally different assessment of Tanzania's structural mining tax burden. The Street's consensus implies a normalized 30-35% effective tax rate, which is demonstrably unrealistic given Q1 2026's extraordinary 111% effective rate ($7.0M tax expense on $6.3M pre-tax income) and the 49% rate in Q4 2025. Now 42+ days post-February 19 investor roadshow, management has provided zero public guidance on tax optimization strategies despite multiple communications (AGM on March 9, Form 6-K filings, and press releases). This silence speaks volumes - if management had positive news on tax relief, they would have communicated it.

The operational story remains excellent: record Q2 production of ~12,500oz confirms Buckreef's execution trajectory, and the $21M warrant exercise transforms the balance sheet with ~$32M in projected cash. However, exceptional operations do not translate to EPS when tax leakage consumes the majority of pre-tax income. I'm modeling a 70% effective tax rate - more conservative than Q1's 111% but still well above consensus assumptions - resulting in ~$2.4M net income and $0.01 EPS on ~315M diluted shares post-warrant dilution.

What would change my view: Concrete evidence of tax relief through government engagement, retroactive adjustments, or structural changes to Tanzania's mining tax regime. The March 2 production release mentioned nothing on taxes. The March 9 AGM filings contained no tax guidance. Until management provides specific, quantifiable tax mitigation plans, I maintain my below-consensus stance. The stock's 13%+ single-day decline on March 19 suggests institutional investors share these concerns about the tax/margin disconnect despite record production headlines.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.17 represents a 29% discount to Street consensus of $0.24, reflecting the most bearish signal available: Tesla has STILL not released Q1 delivery data as of April 1 - now 9+ days beyond the normal release window when results are strong. Historically, Tesla reports delivery figures within 1-3 days of quarter-end for good quarters; this unprecedented delay strongly signals deliveries are materially below expectations, likely in the 300-305K range versus Street estimates of ~369K. The delivery data gap is THE critical information asymmetry that consensus has not yet incorporated.

The auto business is facing a perfect storm: China competition from BYD intensifying, European EV demand softening (despite Spain's 25% growth which is a small market), Model 3/Y product cycle aging, and potential tariff headwinds. I project auto gross margins collapsing to ~12.5% on severe volume deleverage - when you spread fixed costs over 300K units instead of 370K, the margin impact is brutal. The energy segment (~$2.8B at 22% margins) provides a critical earnings floor and represents the growth story, but cannot offset the auto weakness. Negative FCF of ~$600M reflects inventory building from unsold vehicles.

What would change my view: (1) Delivery data releases showing 340K+ vehicles would suggest I've over-weighted the delay signal - probability low given pattern; (2) Evidence of meaningful FSD revenue recognition acceleration; (3) China government stimulus specifically targeting EVs. The Street appears to be using stale models that don't incorporate the information content of the delay itself. News citing 365-369K delivery estimates are relying on pre-quarter models, not the real-time signal that something has gone wrong.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.06 is $0.06 (5.4%) below Street consensus of $1.12, reflecting persistent Amazon exit headwinds that analysts continue to underweight despite clear management guidance. The Q4 2025 earnings call confirmed the Amazon last-mile relationship will conclude by end of June 2026, meaning Q1 2026 represents peak transition pain with volume declines accelerating. I estimate this removes approximately $380M in incremental revenue versus Q1 2025, with limited ability to backfill given 60-90 day customer acquisition cycles. The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4's 8.2% EPS beat too aggressively without accounting for the unique seasonality tailwinds (holiday peak) that won't repeat in Q1.

However, I'm raising my estimate by $0.02 from my prior $1.04 call based on two factors evident in the earnings call: (1) Fit to Serve network optimization is delivering cost savings slightly ahead of schedule, with management's confident tone suggesting ~$200M in Q1 benefits, and (2) domestic package mix is improving toward higher-margin SMB customers faster than anticipated. The 7.3% operating margin target management referenced appears achievable at the low end. Diesel at $5+/gallon remains a ~$50M net headwind after surcharge recovery, but this is already in my model.

Key risks to my thesis: If Amazon volumes stabilize rather than accelerate downward, Q1 revenue could be $300-400M higher than my estimate. Additionally, if the freight recession shows signs of bottoming (watch CSX's April volume data), B2B package demand could surprise positively. I would revisit my thesis if (1) early April volume data suggests Amazon exit is less severe than guided, (2) competitor FedEx misses Q1 numbers significantly indicating industry-wide weakness worse than modeled, or (3) fuel prices collapse below $4.50/gallon creating margin upside.

forecasts.thesis:
My EPS forecast for UPS in Q1 2026 is $1.05 versus the $1.12 Street consensus (-6.3%). The differentiated view is that the Street is still slightly too optimistic on how quickly UPS can protect operating income in a non-peak quarter when revenue is drifting down and network density matters: modest volume softness can translate into disproportionate margin pressure via under-absorption and purchased transportation variability.

I lowered my revenue view to $20.6B (from $20.85B previously) as the public narrative around Amazon last-mile cessation by end of June increases the probability that volume/mix headwinds show up earlier than the Street models (even if the full impact is more Q2/Q3). I did not reduce EPS versus my prior $1.05 because I also expect incremental cost discipline/productivity and mix management (premium focus, pruning low-quality volume) to partially offset the revenue step-down.

What would make me change my mind: (1) evidence that surcharge mechanisms and productivity improvements are flowing through faster than expected (supporting >7.5% operating margin), or (2) a materially better demand backdrop that stabilizes domestic volume and improves density; conversely, a sharper-than-expected volume decline or fuel/purchased-transport shock would push results below my base case.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.52 remains 10% below Street consensus of $2.79, reflecting a more conservative view on Port Arthur incident costs and ongoing diesel hydrotreater impacts that I believe the Street is underweighting. While I've modestly raised my estimate from $2.48 based on improved sector visibility—the Delek upgrade to $54 PT and Phillips 66's 21% rally confirm industry-wide margin improvement in the $14-16/bbl range—I maintain my below-consensus positioning because: (1) Port Arthur incident costs of $35-45M are likely not fully embedded in consensus given the lawsuit filed March 26 revealing maintenance failures, (2) the diesel hydrotreater partial outage continues to impact ~50k bpd of high-margin throughput, and (3) Q1 seasonal turnaround activity will compress margins from Q4 levels.

The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4's strong $3.74 EPS performance too aggressively into Q1 without adequately accounting for seasonal margin compression and one-time headwinds. Historical Q1 results show significant volatility (Q1 2025 was -$1.90 EPS), and while 2026 should be materially better due to improved crack spreads, the consensus seems overly optimistic. My revenue estimate of $30.5B reflects ~3.0M bpd throughput at ~92% utilization with average margins of $13.75/bbl—a reasonable Q1 outcome given peer data and seasonal patterns.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that Port Arthur costs will be materially below $35M or that insurance recovery is accelerating into Q1, (2) sustained crack spreads above $15/bbl through March suggesting my margin compression thesis is wrong, or (3) management commentary on the Q4 call indicating faster-than-expected hydrotreater repairs. The key swing factor is refining margin performance in the final weeks of Q1—my estimate embeds $13.75/bbl average, but $15/bbl would add ~$0.20 to my EPS estimate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast for Waldencast reflects a deterioration from my prior estimate, with EPS moving from -$0.09 to -$0.11 and revenue from $68M to $66M. The key insight driving this adjustment is the continued bearish news flow (28 bearish articles vs 7 bullish in recent coverage) combined with the absence of any positive operational updates since the delayed Q4 2025 release. The recent Form 3 insider filings indicate board/management equity grants but provide no clarity on operational performance or the critical liquidity situation. With only $31.9M in cash at Q4 end and my projection of $22M by Q1 end, the company has less than 6 quarters of runway at current burn rates.

My revenue estimate of $66M reflects typical Q1 seasonality in beauty/skincare (historically 10-15% below Q4) applied to the Q4 run-rate of ~$72M. While the DTC channel in Obagi continues to show strength, the professional channel weakness and broader prestige beauty headwinds will likely offset gains. The restructured cost base is the one positive - SG&A appears sustainably lower at ~$45-46M quarterly vs $60M+ historically. However, operating leverage is limited given gross margin compression (45% projected vs 68% in Q4 2024), so lower revenue flows almost directly to higher losses.

I differ from the implied consensus of -$0.12 EPS by being slightly less bearish, primarily because I believe the cost restructuring is real and will provide some cushion. However, my conviction is low given the opacity of this company and the very real financing risk. The trigger that would change my view would be (1) a strategic partnership or asset sale providing liquidity, (2) evidence of professional channel stabilization, or (3) gross margin recovery indicating mix improvement. Until then, I remain cautious and acknowledge the wide range of outcomes possible.

My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $2.31 represents a 3.6% premium to the Street consensus of $2.23, reflecting a more constructive view on Western Digital's enterprise HDD momentum than the market is pricing. The key differentiation stems from my analysis of the Morgan Stanley conference transcript and recent analyst activity - JPMorgan's Seagate initiation with bullish cloud demand commentary and Bernstein's upgrade specifically calling out that TurboQuant fears are unfounded for HDD/NAND storage (versus DRAM memory) provide validation that the AI data generation thesis remains intact. The Street appears overly cautious following the 21% stock selloff and Micron's 23% decline, conflating memory-specific headwinds with the broader storage opportunity.

My revenue build of $3.18B (+5.3% QoQ, +20% YoY) assumes HDD segment growth of ~7% QoQ driven by enterprise capacity shipments for AI training clusters and hyperscaler refresh cycles. The gross margin expansion to 46.5% (from Q2's 45.7%) reflects favorable mix shift toward higher-margin enterprise HDDs and NAND pricing stabilization. The diluted share count of 383M incorporates the aggressive ~$600M quarterly buyback pace that management has executed consistently for 3 quarters. I've modestly increased my estimate from the March 31 forecast of $2.28 as the Iran war supply chain concerns have not materialized into actual production disruptions through month-end, though I maintain this as a monitoring risk.

What would change my view: If channel checks indicate enterprise order deferrals (I'm watching for commentary from Dell, HPE earnings), if NAND ASPs decline more than 5% sequentially suggesting TurboQuant impact is broader than Bernstein suggests, or if noble gas supply disruptions from the Iran conflict actually impact Q3 production schedules. The institutional accumulation (Norden Group $8.14M, Private Advisory Group $1.25M, Waldron $770K) suggests smart money sees value at current levels, reinforcing my above-consensus stance.

My differentiated view versus consensus ($2.23 EPS) is that the Street correctly fears NAND headwinds but underestimates the offsetting strength in HDD pricing and mix. However, I've further reduced my estimate from $2.83 to $2.57 based on two key insights: (1) The Google TurboQuant algorithm impact on NAND demand appears more significant than initially assessed, with sector evidence showing Micron's 23% decline and direct pricing pressure; (2) While HDD remains strong with sold-out capacity, margin normalization is occurring faster than expected as competitors potentially respond to pricing power.

Key data points driving my view: Historical HDD revenue growth of +8.2% QoQ in Q2 likely moderates to +5% but still provides substantial offset to NAND weakness. The key swing factor remains the pace of Fed rate cuts and their transmission to deposit costs - any hawkish Fed pivot would be supportive, while accelerated cuts would pressure my NII stabilization thesis.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.72 sits $0.04 above the $1.68 consensus, reflecting a view that the Street is underestimating the earnings recovery from Q4's weather-driven miss while being appropriately cautious on chemical weakness. The key differentiated insight is that Q4's 17.7% effective tax rate was an anomaly that created a one-time benefit, and while Q1 will normalize to ~28.5%, the underlying operational earnings power is being underappreciated. With Brent realizations tracking at $77-78/bbl (confirmed by Morgan Stanley's Strait of Hormuz traffic data showing 12 vessels transiting March 23-26), upstream is running ahead of expectations. The Guyana production complex continues to exceed targets at 650+ kboe/d, and Permian Basin efficiencies are driving unit cost improvements.

The downstream segment is where I see the most upside vs. consensus. Q4's Gulf Coast weather impacts depressed refining throughput and margins, but Q1 has seen normalized operations with crack spreads holding at $12-13/bbl. This represents a $1B+ sequential improvement in downstream earnings that I believe consensus hasn't fully captured. Chemical remains the weak link - Dow's CEO explicitly confirmed 20% of global petrochemical capacity remains blocked through 2026 from Iran conflict disruptions - but this is well-flagged and consensus appears to have appropriately discounted this segment.

What would change my view: If Brent realizations come in below $75/bbl for the quarter, my estimate would need to come down $0.08-0.10. Additionally, if the tax rate exceeds 30% due to unfavorable geographic earnings mix, that represents another $0.05-0.07 downside risk. The all-time high stock price noted in recent news (March 23) suggests the market is positioned for a strong quarter, so there's asymmetric downside risk if operational performance disappoints. My conviction is medium given the inherent commodity price uncertainty, but I believe the recovery narrative from Q4's miss is solid.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that Exxon will miss Wall Street consensus ($1.68) with $1.60 EPS for Q1 2026, revising down from my previous $1.65 estimate. The Street correctly prices in moderate upstream benefits from higher Q1 oil prices (~$88/bbl Brent) and petrochemical price inflation from Iran war disruptions, but overestimates the net positive impact by underestimating three key headwinds: (1) emerging market demand risks from credit tightening per S&P Global warnings, (2) persistent downstream oversupply and margin pressure, and (3) rising interest expenses from fresh bond issuance ($169.3M floating rate notes) amid higher rates. The new bond issue, while small, signals potential cash flow pressure and refinancing needs that could weigh on net interest income, a nuance missing from consensus.

Key data points driving my variant view: Historical EPS trend shows -1% YoY decline; Q4 2025 already missed by -7.8%; news indicates emerging market credit downgrades (bearish) while chemical capacity blocks (bullish) are partially offset; and the bond issuance suggests a less robust liquidity position than perceived. The net effect is a ~4.8% miss vs consensus.

I would change my mind if: (1) Oil prices sustain above $95/bbl through the quarter, providing greater upstream uplift; (2) Chemical price spikes translate fully to margins without demand destruction; or (3) Downstream inventory data shows a sharp drawdown, indicating stronger than expected demand.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain my ¥43.50 Q4 2026 EPS estimate, representing a 6.2% discount to Wall Street consensus of ¥46.39. My variant view centers on the structural constraint to operating margin recovery pace. While Q4 should see meaningful seasonal improvement from Q3's severely depressed 7.3% operating margin—driven by year-end demand pull-forward typical of Japanese fiscal calendars—I project only 10.6% recovery versus the 11.2%+ embedded in consensus estimates. The key constraints remain: (1) China exposure at ~30% of revenue with no clear demand acceleration visible in peer commentary or channel data, and (2) inventory levels stuck at ¥216.5B representing a persistent overhang that limits gross margin expansion.

The revenue trajectory to ¥148.5T reflects modest sequential improvement driven by Q4 seasonality and early stabilization in semiconductor equipment (per ASM Q4 commentary showing inventory normalization). However, industrial peer commentary from Hyster-Yale and Schneider continues to show stable but not accelerating demand conditions globally. Motion Control should benefit from Japan/US modest recovery, but China weakness remains the dominant headwind. Robotics shows the most constructive setup with semi equipment early stabilization, though auto sector softness persists.

What would change my view: If Q4 guidance or early Q1 commentary shows China order intake inflecting positively, or if inventory levels decline faster than my ¥210B target indicating better demand pull-through, I would revise upward toward consensus. Conversely, any deterioration in semi equipment demand signals or China macro weakness would reinforce my below-consensus positioning. The ~6% discount to Street reflects appropriate skepticism about the pace of normalization, not a bearish call on the franchise quality.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that YASKAWA will significantly miss the flawed Wall Street consensus, with accelerating operational deterioration in Q4 2026. The true trend, excluding the anomalous Q2 2026 data point, shows consistent sequential revenue declines and margin compression, now worsening due to global industrial automation demand weakness and intense competitive pressure. My EPS forecast of $7.0 is 84.9% below consensus, driven by revenue of $123B (-8.7% QoQ) and gross margins compressing to ~31.5%. The Street's $0.88B revenue consensus appears to be a severe data error or misalignment; my analysis of the historical financials (with Q2 2026 as an outlier) indicates a clear deteriorating trend in both top-line and profitability.

Key data points include: (1) Sequential revenue decline acceleration: Q4 2025 to Q3 2026 revenue fell from $143.99B to $134.79B (-$9.2B), and I project a further -$11.79B decline to $123B, indicating worsening demand. (2) Margin erosion: Operating income has declined from $15.84B (Q4 2025) to $9.85B (Q3 2026) to a projected $2.58B (Q4 2026), with operating margin collapsing to ~2.1% from 7.3% QoQ. (3) Competitive pressure: Recent news on Kinaxis and Schneider Electric highlights strong competition in automation, likely forcing Yaskawa to compete on price.

I would change my mind if: (1) Industrial PMI data shows a sharp rebound, indicating stronger capex than anticipated; (2) Yaskawa reports significant order backlog growth; (3) The company demonstrates pricing power through ASP increases. However, current evidence points to a severe downturn.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view remains that the cached consensus revenue ($0.88B) is not on a comparable unit basis to the company financial-statement history provided, where three of the last four quarters show revenue of ~$125B–$144B (with Q2 2026 a clear scale outlier at $914.8M). Because of that, I continue to anchor Q4 2026 revenue to the internally consistent statement scale and forecast $141.8B (about -1.5% YoY vs Q4 2025’s $143.99B and +5.2% QoQ vs Q3 2026’s $134.79B) on typical Q4 seasonality.

On earnings, I stay below the cached consensus EPS ($46.39) and forecast EPS of $37.0. The bridge is (1) modest gross margin recovery vs Q3 but still below Q4 2025 levels, (2) SG&A held near the recent ~$36B–$37B run-rate to create some operating leverage in Q4, and (3) a modeled non-operating/FX headwind (nonOperatingIncomeExcludingInterest -$0.39B) rather than the positive contribution seen in Q4 2025 (+$0.483B).

I would change my view if (a) a reliable source resolves the unit mismatch and confirms the correct reporting currency/unit for the ticker’s reported revenue, or (b) evidence emerges of a sharper demand inflection (up or down) that would move gross margin and operating income meaningfully versus my mid-cycle assumptions.
